strengths: Significance: Combining synthesized Python transition models with PDDL-guided bilevel planning is a useful approach to reusable game-playing agents. The reported results span four domains, with successful model reuse across levels and transfer to 40 Baba is AI levels.

Empirical merits: Table 3 provides concrete evidence that hierarchical decomposition accelerates planning on the selected VGDL tasks; for example, Push Boulders level 2 decreases from 432.58 to 30.11 seconds. The heavy-prompting baseline in Table 5 also tests whether supplying additional domain knowledge resolves direct LLM planning failures.

Originality: The distinctive contribution is integrating abstract subgoals with online program-model refinement and exploration. Labeling prediction errors by abstract actions is a plausible mechanism for making model revision easier, even though program synthesis and bilevel planning individually build on established work.

Presentation and limitations: The diagrams and worked examples make the architecture accessible. The paper explicitly acknowledges the burden of manually designing abstractions and the restriction to deterministic environments. The game-based experiments raise no evident material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness of the efficiency claim: Section 4.1 measures sample efficiency using API calls rather than environment interactions. Calls can contain different amounts of experience and computation, and GPT-4o and o1 have different costs. Without transition counts, token usage, and end-to-end runtime, the results establish reduced query usage, not the broader RL sample-efficiency claims motivating the paper.

Insufficient comparison and attribution: The principal baseline generates plans directly with o1. There is no empirical comparison with closely related code-world-model agents such as WorldCoder, or a competitive search-based agent using the same synthesized model and comparable domain information. Table 3 isolates planning speed on two domains, but does not establish that abstraction-guided refinement or exploration improves learning. These require controlled ablations, especially on KekeCompetition where revisions actually occur.

Dependence on supplied task knowledge: Section 3.3 states that both PDDL domain and problem files are hard-coded, and predicate implementations are also supplied. Section 4.4 adds strategically consequential knowledge such as boxes_stuck, maze bottlenecks, and not_near_door. This is a valid restricted setting, but the evaluation does not separate the contribution of these engineered strategies from learned dynamics or establish their transfer to independently selected tasks. The honest limitations discussion does not resolve this evidential gap.

Evaluation reliability: The main success and API-call tables provide no independent synthesis-run counts, uncertainty estimates, or sensitivity to level ordering, despite sampling GPT-4o at temperature 0.7. The five-run averaging applies only to planning runtimes. With 5 Sokoban, 4 Push Boulders, 17 BabyAI, and 13 KekeCompetition levels, unspecified selection procedures further limit conclusions about robustness and generalization.

Reproducibility: The code-availability footnote links only to https://github.com. Appendix A contains prompt templates with unresolved domain-description placeholders, rather than complete experimental prompts. Full PDDL/problem files, checker implementations, exact task identifiers, model snapshots, and execution/reset settings are not provided. These omissions are particularly consequential because the handcrafted components determine the planning decomposition.

Algorithm specification: Algorithm 1 constructs the purported actual replay buffer using the learned transition function rather than environment observations, repeatedly starts BFS from s0 without explicit state propagation, and does not specify a retry after model refinement. More substantively, failed low-level refinement can arise from an infeasible abstract plan or an unfortunate intermediate state, not only an incorrect world model. Backtracking or abstract replanning behavior is unclear. Equation 2 also omits delete effects despite operators that explicitly have them.

Scope of the conclusions: Transfer across visually distinct games is overstated for an agent receiving symbolic text states; the transfer experiment needs details about representation adapters and changes to supplied abstractions. Likewise, comparison with EMPA is historical rather than controlled. Overall, the promising integration and selected-task results do not yet outweigh the missing controls and reproducibility details needed to support the central claims.

strengths: Significance: Combining reusable Python world models with PDDL-guided bilevel planning is a useful direction for reducing repeated LLM queries and making symbolic model-based agents more practical.

Empirical merits: Tables 1–5 report successful completion of all evaluated levels across four domains, with substantially fewer API calls than direct o1 planning. Table 3 provides concrete evidence that hierarchical decomposition accelerates search, including solving instances where the flat planner exceeds 500 seconds.

Originality: Although program synthesis of world models and bilevel planning are established ideas, using abstract subplans both to organize search and to contextualize model-revision feedback is a potentially valuable integration. The reported transfer to 40 Baba Is AI levels is also encouraging.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture diagrams and worked revision examples make the intended approach understandable. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges hand-engineered abstractions and the restriction to deterministic domains. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—sample efficiency is not established by the reported metric. Section 4.1 measures sample efficiency through API calls rather than environment interactions. Calls can contain different amounts of experience and require different token budgets; exploration and execution costs are not reported. These results support reduced LLM-query usage, but not the broader claims about RL sample efficiency or human-like learning.

Soundness—comparisons do not isolate the central contribution. The main baseline directly generates plans without an external search algorithm, whereas TheoryCoder receives Fast Downward, BFS, and engineered symbolic structure. The heavy-prompting baseline is useful but still lacks executable search. There is no empirical comparison with closely related code-world-model methods such as WorldCoder, and the flat-planning ablation measures runtime only on two domains. Consequently, the claimed learning benefits of abstraction-guided refinement remain unsupported by a controlled ablation. EMPA is discussed through historical results rather than a matched evaluation.

Significance and generality depend heavily on supplied task knowledge. Section 3.3 explicitly states that both domain and problem files are hard-coded, and Python predicate implementations are supplied. Section 4.4 adds strategic constraints such as boxes_stuck and not_near_door, plus maze bottleneck decomposition. These encode substantial problem-solving knowledge. The issue is not the acknowledged use of hand engineering itself, but the absence of controls or a sufficiently complete specification showing how much performance comes from these inputs versus learned dynamics.

Technical specification has material inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 uses the learned transition model to populate the supposedly actual replay buffer, starts each subplan search from s0, and does not explicitly update the execution state or repeat planning after model refinement. Equation 2 omits delete effects despite operators that require them. More fundamentally, failure to refine a high-level plan can reflect an infeasible abstraction or an unfortunate intermediate state even with correct dynamics; the method does not clearly specify backtracking or high-level replanning. These issues prevent the written algorithm from reliably specifying the claimed procedure.

Evaluation reliability is insufficiently characterized. The main comparison covers only 5 Sokoban, 4 Push Boulders, 17 BabyAI, and 13 KekeCompetition levels. Selection criteria and independent synthesis-run counts are not specified, and success/API results lack uncertainty estimates despite GPT-4o sampling at temperature 0.7. Five repetitions are stated only for runtime measurements. Because models accumulate knowledge across levels, level ordering and variation across independent learning runs are particularly important.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The code-availability footnote links only to https://github.com. Appendix A gives prompt templates but leaves domain descriptions and other substantive inputs as placeholders; complete baseline prompts, PDDL files, predicate/checker implementations, exact level identifiers, model snapshots, and planner configuration are not supplied. These omissions are consequential because the engineered representations and interface code determine much of the method's behavior.

Transfer claims exceed the documented evidence. Section 4.6 reports successful transfer to all 40 Baba Is AI levels but does not detail representation adapters, target-domain abstractions, or per-level results. Because the agent consumes symbolic states, visual differences alone do not establish substantive transfer. Claims about arbitrary goal/color changes and broad compositionality need systematic controlled tests.

strengths: Originality: Combining synthesized Python dynamics with PDDL-guided planning and abstraction-labeled model revision is a useful integration. The contribution is primarily architectural, with a plausible mechanism for making learned world models more practical.

Significance: The reported results are promising across four puzzle domains. TheoryCoder solves the evaluated levels with substantially fewer LLM calls, and the reported transfer to 40 Baba is AI levels without further model learning suggests useful reuse of learned mechanics.

Soundness: Table 3 provides direct evidence that hierarchical decomposition accelerates planning on the selected VGDL tasks. For example, Push Boulders level 2 improves from 432.58 to 30.11 seconds; timings are averaged over five runs.

Presentation and limitations: The diagrams and worked examples make the architecture accessible. The conclusion explicitly acknowledges handcrafted abstractions and the restriction to deterministic environments. These are appropriate disclosures, and the game-based experiments raise no evident material ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—sample efficiency is not established by the chosen metric. Section 4.1 counts API calls rather than environment transitions or episodes, omitting exploration and execution data. Calls also differ in model, token usage, and computation. The results support reduced query counts, but not the broader RL sample-efficiency claims or a complete efficiency comparison.

Soundness—important prior knowledge is supplied manually. Section 3.3 states that both domain and problem files are hard-coded and predicate checkers are provided. Section 4.4 adds strategic constraints such as boxes_stuck, not_near_door, and maze bottlenecks. These can encode substantial solution knowledge. The paper does not adequately separate benefits of learning dynamics from benefits of this engineering, or establish that abstractions were fixed independently of evaluation levels.

Evaluation and originality: The principal baseline directly generates action sequences, whereas TheoryCoder receives an external search procedure and reusable symbolic models. Heavy prompting in KekeCompetition is helpful but does not resolve this difference. Comparisons against closely related code-world-model agents, such as the cited WorldCoder, and controlled ablations of abstraction-guided exploration and revision are missing. The runtime ablation alone does not establish the claimed improvement in learning convergence.

Reliability and generalization: Success and API-call tables lack repeated synthesis runs or uncertainty estimates despite GPT-4o temperature 0.7; only runtime measurements explicitly average five runs. Level selection and abstraction-development protocols are insufficiently specified. The transfer result is encouraging, but visually different games do not test visual robustness when the agent receives symbolic text states, and the state adapters and transferred versus newly supplied abstractions are not documented.

Technical specification: Algorithm 1 generates the supposedly actual replay buffer using the learned transition model rather than the environment, repeatedly starts BFS from s0, and omits clear state advancement and retry logic after refinement. Equation 2 ignores delete effects despite operators using them. More substantively, greedy refinement of successive abstract subplans can leave later subplans infeasible; backtracking or alternative-plan handling is not specified. These issues obstruct a faithful implementation, even if some are pseudocode errors.

Reproducibility: The code link points only to https://github.com. Appendix A supplies prompt templates but leaves domain descriptions as placeholders and omits complete baseline prompts, PDDL files, predicate implementations, exact model snapshots, and sufficient benchmark configuration. Together with the methodological gaps, this prevents others from reliably reproducing and attributing the reported gains. The promising integration needs stronger controlled evidence and implementation disclosure before acceptance.

strengths: Originality: Combining an LLM-synthesized Python transition model with PDDL-guided bilevel planning is a useful integration. Using abstract subplan labels to organize model-revision feedback provides an interesting connection between planning representations and model learning.

Significance: The reported results demonstrate promising reuse of learned dynamics across levels. TheoryCoder solves the evaluated Sokoban, Push Boulders, BabyAI, and KekeCompetition levels with substantially fewer LLM queries than direct planning.

Soundness: Table 4 provides concrete evidence that decomposition can accelerate planning on the selected VGDL tasks: Sokoban level 4 decreases from 149.70 seconds without abstractions to 0.40 seconds with them. The WorldCoder comparison also goes beyond an LLM-only baseline.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture diagrams and worked revision examples make the central approach accessible. Sections 4.7 and 5 candidly discuss initialization failures, unsuccessful harder levels, handcrafted abstractions, and restricted environments. The custom-game experiment provides some evidence beyond familiar benchmarks. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—unquantified reliability: The principal success rates and query counts lack repeated-run distributions, seed counts, or uncertainty estimates. This is consequential because synthesis uses temperature 0.7 and Section 4.7 explicitly reports runs that become stuck and require restarting. The manuscript does not explain how such runs contribute to the reported 100% success rates or query budgets. Averaging planning runtimes over five runs does not establish learning reliability.

Soundness—contribution attribution: The supplied knowledge includes hard-coded domain and problem files, Python predicate implementations, and strategically informative constraints such as boxes_stuck, not_near_door, and maze bottlenecks (Sections 3.3 and 4.4). These are substantial sources of task knowledge. Their use is legitimate, but the experiments do not adequately separate their contribution from learned dynamics or hierarchical feedback. The runtime ablation does not establish that abstraction improves learning; a matched model-learning ablation without abstract feedback and exploration is needed.

Evaluation—sample efficiency: Section 4.1 primarily equates sample efficiency with API-call count. Queries differ in token usage and computation, and TheoryCoder additionally uses simulator search and environment interactions. Environment-step comparisons appear only for the two VGDL games, while token comparisons with WorldCoder cover another subset. The evidence supports reduced query usage more directly than broad claims of improved RL sample efficiency.

Methodological specification: Algorithm 1 does not explicitly advance the starting state between subplans, specify recovery when BFS fails, or return to planning after the model update on line 17. More fundamentally, greedily selecting one realization of each abstract subgoal can prevent subsequent subgoals even with correct dynamics; no backtracking procedure is described. Equation 2 omits delete effects, and Figure 8's movement operator adds the destination without deleting the origin. These issues leave the implemented planner and its failure handling insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility and baseline assessment: Appendix A gives prompt templates but omits the instantiated domain descriptions that determine how much mechanics knowledge is supplied. Complete domain/problem files, checker implementations, exact level identifiers, model snapshots, hardware, and Fast Downward configurations are not provided. The WorldCoder comparison specifies an MCTS depth of 30 but does not establish comparable search resources or provide enough detail to assess sensitivity to that choice.

Significance and originality: The main advance is an integration of established program-synthesis and bilevel-planning ideas. The small, domain-tailored evaluations demonstrate potential, but do not yet establish a broadly reusable advance over existing code-world-model methods. The custom-game result is encouraging but lacks a comparative baseline and repeated trials; it cannot exclude contamination effects in the original benchmarks.

Presentation: The intuitive explanation is stronger than the formal account. Section 3.3 conflates the inverse of an action abstraction with the state-abstraction notation, and several cross-references are incorrect. Together with the algorithmic omissions, this makes faithful implementation difficult. Overall, the promising integration and selected speedups do not outweigh the unresolved reliability, attribution, and reproducibility weaknesses.

strengths: Originality: Combining LLM-synthesized Python transition models with PDDL-guided bilevel planning is a useful integration. Abstract subplan labels also provide a plausible mechanism for directing model revision toward particular mechanics.

Significance: The reported results demonstrate promising reuse of learned dynamics across levels. TheoryCoder solves the evaluated Sokoban and Push Boulders levels with one synthesis call per game, and Table 7 reports 100% success with 69,402 tokens versus WorldCoder’s 83% with 388,861 tokens.

Soundness: Table 4 provides direct evidence that hierarchical decomposition can substantially accelerate planning on these instances. For example, Sokoban level 4 takes 0.40 seconds with abstractions versus 149.70 seconds without them. Timing results are averaged over five runs.

Presentation and limitations: The architecture diagrams and worked examples make the main idea accessible. Sections 4.7 and 5 candidly discuss initialization failures, unsuccessful harder levels, and the burden of engineering abstractions. The custom-game experiment is a useful additional check on dependence on familiar benchmarks. No material research-ethics concern is apparent in the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—uncontrolled contribution of supplied knowledge: Section 3.3.1 states that both PDDL domain and problem files are hard-coded, and Python predicate checkers are supplied. These encode substantial task knowledge: avoiding stuck boxes, identifying maze bottlenecks, and keeping dropped keys away from doors (Section 4.4). The paper does not adequately separate the benefit of this engineering from learned world models or hierarchical planning. The timing ablation supports decomposition benefits, but there is no corresponding controlled ablation of abstraction-guided exploration and revision to substantiate improved learning convergence.

Soundness—success rates lack a reproducible statistical basis: Most success and API-call results have no stated number of independent synthesis runs, uncertainty estimates, or restart policy, despite GPT-4o sampling at temperature 0.7. Section 4.7 explicitly reports runs that become stuck and require restarting. Without quantifying their frequency and explaining how these runs enter the reported results, the 100% success figures do not establish reliable performance. Averaging planning runtime over five runs does not resolve this issue.

Evaluation—API efficiency is conflated with sample efficiency: Section 4.1 primarily measures sample efficiency by API calls, although a call can incorporate different amounts of environment experience, prompt context, and computation. Environment-step results are supplied only for the two VGDL games, and broader comparisons omit consistent interaction, token, and end-to-end compute accounting. The results support reduced query usage more directly than the broader claims about sample-efficient learning.

Evaluation—baseline comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the advance: Direct action generation by o1 differs from TheoryCoder in both planning machinery and supplied symbolic structure. The heavily prompted Keke baseline is informative, but still does not isolate the value of learning a model versus using an external planner. The closer WorldCoder comparison is limited to one curriculum with a maximum MCTS depth of 30, without sensitivity analysis or a justification that this setting is adequate. Fast Downward search configuration and encoding details are also missing, limiting conclusions about superiority over classical planning.

Reproducibility and methodological precision: Appendix A provides templates with unfilled domain-description and state placeholders, rather than the complete experimental prompts. Complete PDDL files, predicate checkers, benchmark seeds or level identifiers, exact API model versions, and hardware/search settings are not supplied. Algorithm 1 repeatedly calls BFS from s0 without showing state advancement, omits the retry loop after model refinement, and leaves handling of infeasible subplans unclear. Equation 2 omits delete effects despite operators elsewhere using them. These omissions make the implemented procedure difficult to reconstruct.

Significance and scope: The main evaluations use small, selected collections of deterministic, symbolically observed levels with domain-specific abstractions. They establish a promising specialized system, but provide limited evidence for broadly transferable abstractions or scalable learning in new domains. The custom game reduces concern that its exact levels were memorized; it does not exclude reliance on pretrained knowledge of familiar mechanics. Relative to prior code-world-model and bilevel-planning work, the integration could be useful, but stronger controlled and repeated evaluation is needed before its central claims can reliably support further research.

strengths: Originality: TheoryCoder offers a useful integration of LLM-synthesized Python dynamics with PDDL abstractions, hierarchical planning, and abstraction-labeled model revision. The contribution lies in connecting these components, particularly using the same abstractions for planning and exploration.

Significance: The reported planning improvements are substantial. In Table 4, Sokoban level 4 takes 0.40 seconds with bilevel planning versus 149.70 seconds without it; several other instances become solvable within the timeout. Reusing synthesized models across levels without additional LLM calls is also practically valuable.

Presentation: The architecture diagrams, concrete abstraction examples, and model-revision walkthroughs make the main idea understandable. Comparisons include direct LLM planning, EMPA, WorldCoder, and a planning ablation, providing several useful perspectives.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript candidly discusses hand-engineered abstractions, initialization failures, and two harder levels that remain unsolved. The custom-game experiment is a useful check against dependence on memorized benchmark implementations. The game-based experiments raise no apparent material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness—reliability of the headline results: Success rates and API-call totals lack reported distributions across independent synthesis runs, despite GPT-4o being sampled at temperature 0.7. Section 4.7 explicitly reports runs that become stuck and require restarting, but does not quantify their frequency or explain whether restarts enter the reported results. Table 4 averages planning runtimes over five runs, which does not establish end-to-end learning reliability. The reported 100% success therefore needs substantially clearer accounting.

Soundness—attribution to learned models versus supplied knowledge: Section 3.3.1 states that both PDDL domain and problem files are hard-coded, and Python predicate checkers are also supplied. These encode consequential strategies, including avoiding stuck boxes, navigating selected bottlenecks, and keeping dropped keys away from doorways. The experiments do not adequately separate gains from this engineering from gains in model learning or abstraction-guided refinement. A matched-information comparison and separate ablations of planning, exploration, and revision guidance are needed.

Evaluation—sample-efficiency claims exceed the measurements: API calls primarily measure query usage, not environmental sample efficiency. A call can contain different amounts of experience and computation, and a reusable-model agent can naturally make zero subsequent calls while a direct planner must produce new plans. Environment-step measurements are limited to the VGDL tasks, and comprehensive token and end-to-end runtime accounting is absent. The WorldCoder comparison is relevant, but the effects of its depth-30 MCTS configuration and unequal abstraction access are not established.

Reproducibility: Appendix A provides prompt templates but leaves domain descriptions and actual inputs as placeholders. The manuscript does not provide complete PDDL problem files, predicate/checker implementations, baseline prompts, exact model snapshots, hardware, or Fast Downward search settings. Exploration selection, reset behavior, and the identities of several evaluated levels are insufficiently specified. These omissions matter because the supplied abstractions and execution protocol strongly influence performance.

Methodological specification: Algorithm 1 repeatedly calls BFS from s0 without explicitly propagating the current state, lacks an explicit retry after model refinement, and leaves failed low-level searches insufficiently defined. Equation 2 adds positive effects without accounting for delete effects, although the presented operators use them. More substantively, greedily concatenating subplans can reach intermediate states from which later subplans are impossible; backtracking or recovery from this situation is not explained.

Significance and scope: The results support a promising, engineered solution for selected deterministic grid-world curricula, but do not yet establish broad generalization or scalable theory learning. The custom game helps address contamination concerns without excluding them for the original benchmarks. Given existing program-world-model and bilevel-planning work, stronger controlled evidence is necessary to establish the incremental contribution. The decisive concerns are the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility gaps, rather than the honestly acknowledged limitations.
